tagline: A great sheltered bay with island reserves an easy crossing from the capital
summary: Maputo sits on the western shore of one of southern Africa's largest natural bays, a calm, swell-protected body of water framed by the capital, the southern district of Catembe, and the marine reserve of Inhaca Island at its mouth. For decades the only link to Catembe was a crowded ferry; the 2018 Maputo–Catembe bridge changed the road picture but left the bay's leisure and island corridors underserved. Inhaca Island — a biodiverse marine reserve with beaches and a research station — lies about thirteen nautical miles offshore and is reached today by an infrequent, slow ferry. The bay's shelter, the capital's growing waterfront, and Mozambique's beach-tourism ambitions make Maputo a natural node for scheduled island links and on-demand bay mobility that no modern operator provides.

transit_planning: Maputo's recent transport investment centred on the Catembe bridge and ring road, reshaping road access south of the bay. The water corridors to Inhaca and the bay's islands remain served by legacy ferries and charter boats — a structured marine layer adds the island and leisure links the road programme does not reach.

competitive_landscape: The Maputo–Inhaca link is served by an infrequent, slow ferry; bay leisure and island day-trips rely on ad-hoc charter. No modern, scheduled passenger-vessel operator works the bay. The Catembe bridge absorbed the main road crossing but left the island and leisure water corridors open — a clear structural gap for organised marine mobility.
seasonality: The cooler dry season (May–October) offers the calmest bay conditions and is peak for island tourism; the November–April wet season brings heat, humidity and occasional cyclonic swell at the bay mouth that can disrupt the Inhaca crossing. The inner bay stays sheltered year-round.
regulatory_note: Mozambique's maritime passenger transport is overseen by the national maritime authority (INAMAR); the existing Inhaca and Catembe ferries operate under licence, so a modern operator enters an established frame. Inhaca's marine-reserve status means island access is coordinated with conservation authorities, favouring low-wake, low-impact craft.
